deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The page reduces the reciprocal zenith-distance (trigonometric levelling) observations of 1825 in the western part of the Hannover triangulation: Brillit, Bremerlehe, Garlste, Varel, Langwarden, Jever. It gives one height difference per line. The next folio uses these as the observations ('beobachtet') in a least-squares adjustment of the heights of the principal triangle points ('Ausgleichung der Höhen der Hauptdreieckspunkte'). The 4.6 entry +16.112, 4.5 +26.921, 1.4 +1.147, etc. reappear there verbatim. The same reciprocal data are then reused to derive a mean coefficient of terrestrial refraction for 1825, and for comparison for 1823 (the Hamburg–Lüneburg stations of the degree measurement). The 'Kr.' annotations are most likely by L. Krüger, editor of Werke IX.

PART 1: one line per station of a reciprocal pair (A observes B, B observes A).

The columns, as I decode them:
- i = instrument height (0.322 m almost everywhere; 0.105 at Jever).
- t = height of the signal/heliotrope observed.
- n = number of observations (20; 26 at Garlste).
- delta = observed depression below the horizon (written -m' s'').
- c = reduction for unequal instrument and signal heights, c = (i - t)/s * rho with rho = 206265 (my identification; verified numerically on every line). Example: Brillit (0.322 - 0.324)/31717.6*rho = -0.013''.
- Third numeric column: the reduced angle in seconds, e = -delta + c. Example: -485.562 - 0.013 = -485.575; Garlste -641.673 + 0.202 = -641.471.
- log s: the log of the side in metres (e.g. 4.50130 gives s = 31717.6 m).
- Final column: the height difference.

The height difference follows from the classical reciprocal formula, which eliminates refraction (assumed equal at both ends) and earth curvature:
  Delta h(A - B) = s * tan((e_B... ) ) ~ s * (|e_A| - |e_B|)/(2 rho).
The station with the larger depression is the higher one.

All eight pairs, my recomputation:
- Brillit–Bremerlehe: (485.575 - 276.013)/2 = 104.781''; 31717.6 * 104.781/206265 = 16.112. ✓
- Garlste–Bremerlehe: (641.471 - 320.834)/2 = 160.3185''; s = 10^4.53957 ≈ 34640, giving 26.92. ✓ The corrected value replaces a crossed-out 650.898 / +27.764.
- Garlste–Varel: 62.050'' * 41359/rho = 12.441. ✓
- Bremerlehe–Varel: (573.874 - 414.719)/2 = 79.5775''; * 35676/rho = 13.764. Written -13.764 (Bremerlehe lower). ✓
- Bremerlehe–Langwarden: 309.912'' is reduced by +26.449''. That is 1.497'' height reduction (0.322 - 0.182 m) plus ~24.95'', presumably a centring/eccentricity reduction; the 0.182 is struck out. Then (283.463 - 258.946)/2 = 12.2585''; * 19294/rho = 1.147. ✓ A bracketed alternative log s 4.28464 is also noted.
- Varel–Langwarden: (487.539 - 238.836)/2 = 124.3515''; * 25644/rho = 15.460. ✓
- Langwarden–Jever: (426.800 - 317.608)/2 = 54.596''; * 27070/rho = 7.165. Written -7.165 (Jever higher). ✓
- Varel–Jever: (373.711 - 310.236)/2 = 31.7375''; * 24886/rho = 3.829. ✓

The absolute datum is 'Höhe von Langwarden über dem Meer 24.724 m' (24.726 on the next folio).

PART 2: refraction coefficient, 1825. For each pair the table gives four columns:
- C = central (geocentric) angle s/R in arcseconds. Implied R ≈ 6.386–6.389 × 10^6 m, a radius of curvature appropriate to latitude ~53°.
- D = |e_A| + |e_B|, the sum of reduced reciprocal depressions.
- r = C - D, the total refraction at both ends.
- k_i = r/C.

This rests on the reciprocal relation delta_A + delta_B = C - (rho_A + rho_B). With rho_A = rho_B = (k/2) C this gives k = (C - D)/C, the modern refraction coefficient (ratio of earth radius to radius of the light ray).

Totals: Sum C = 7763.012 and Sum r = 1228.541. Hence k_1825 = Sum r / Sum C = 0.15826. This is a mean of the k_i weighted by C, i.e. by distance; it is equivalent to least squares with error variance proportional to distance.

PART 3: same for 1823. Timpenberg, Nindorf, Wilsede to Hamburg and Lüneburg. Sum C = 6105.219 and Sum r = 862.415, giving k_1823 = 0.14126.

RIGHT MARGIN. This is the edge of the following folio: the list of adjusted station heights (Langwarden 24.726 … Deister 307.912) and the coefficient patterns of the normal equations.
errors: Langwarden–Jever and Varel–Jever rows: the depression sums D are interchanged. 317.608 + 426.800 = 744.408 belongs to Langwarden–Jever; 373.711 + 310.236 = 683.947 belongs to Varel–Jever. The C values are correctly assigned (s = 27070 m gives ≈874'', s = 24886 m gives ≈804''). Correct values: Langwarden–Jever r = 129.364, k = 0.148; Varel–Jever r = 120.457, k = 0.150. The page instead has 189.825 (0.22) and 59.996 (0.07), so these two apparent outliers are artefacts. The total Sum r = 1228.541, and hence k = 0.15826, is unaffected.

Varel (Bremerlehe–Varel pair): 9'32.862'' - 0.012 gives -572.874, but -573.874 is written and used. It is used both in Delta h = -13.764 and in D = 988.593. Either the angle should read 9'33.862'' (possible misreading) or there is a 1'' slip. With 572.874 the results would be -13.678 m and r = 164.718.
Brillit–Bremerlehe k = 262.891/1024.479 = 0.2566, written 0.25: truncated rather than rounded. Trivial.
Nindorf–Lüneburg: 445.338 - 397.994 = 47.344, written 47.342. A 0.002'' slip with negligible effect on 0.14126.

Varel (Varel–Langwarden pair): the correction +0.286 does not match (0.322 - 0.288)/25644*rho = 0.273. The 0.288 is struck out; the replacement signal height (≈0.286 m) is not legible. Not an error per se.
Annotation 'Brief an Bessel vom 27 Octbr 1846' cannot be right: Bessel died 17 March 1846. The year must be 1826 (or another year), or the reading is wrong.

results.what: Height differences from reciprocal (simultaneous-type) zenith distances, Delta h = s*(e_A - e_B)/(2 rho), after reducing for instrument and signal heights (i - t)/s*rho.
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th/19th-century geodesy (Delambre, Gauss, Bessel and others)

results.what: Coefficient of terrestrial refraction from reciprocal depressions, k = (C - (delta_A + delta_B))/C, averaged as Sum r / Sum C. Gives 0.15826 for 1825 and 0.14126 for 1823.
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Hannover degree measurement, k ≈ 0.13) and Bessel (East Prussian arc); the concept goes back to Lambert/Delambre

results.what: Use of these height differences as observations in a least-squares adjustment of the station heights (on the next folio).
results.modern_name: Least-squares adjustment of a levelling network

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine geodetic reduction work from the Hannover survey. Reciprocal trigonometric levelling and Gauss's determination of the refraction coefficient are well documented, partly published and in Werke IX. Only the specific numbers, and the row-swap slip that does not affect the final result, are unpublished detail.

checkable.asserts: Equals -1.000, exposing the 1'' discrepancy in the Varel line
(744.408, 683.947): the D values for Langwarden–Jever and Varel–Jever are swapped on the page
Implied earth radius ≈ 6.386e6 m used for the central angles

transcription_corrections: Third-column entries are reduced angles in seconds, e = -delta + c (e.g. -641.471 = -641.673 + 0.202). The '{+41.673+}' insertion means the angle reads 10'41.673''.
Varel line of the Bremerlehe–Varel pair: the image angle may read 9'33.862'', consistent with -573.874; the transcription has 9'32.862''.
The two columns of small numbers +0.322 / +0.324 etc. are instrument and signal heights in metres. The heading 'Höhe der …' over them probably reads 'Höhe des Instr.' or similar.
'(vergl. Br. an Bessel vom 27 Octbr 1846)': the year is probably 1826 or misread, since Bessel died in March 1846.

Right margin is the edge of the next folio. Brillit there is 44.584 (not 44.534), Bremen 82.882 (22.882 struck out), Bötel 52.441, Brüttendorf 49.631, Hamburg 129.370, Elmhorst 89.990, Wulfsode 104.510, as on the next page.
Langwarden in the Bremerlehe pair: correction is -0.021, i.e. (0.322 - 0.324)/19294*rho.
